title: Does the first bulb use up the current?
hook: Two bulbs share one battery. Does the second one get the leftovers?

knows: wires connect them in a loop
that amps and volts are electrical units
doesNotKnow: the difference between current and energy

misconception: Current is used up by the first bulb, so less of it reaches the second bulb and less still returns to the battery.
objective: The learner can explain that in a single loop the same current passes every point, and that what bulbs use up is energy (voltage drop), not current.

claims.text: In a single series loop the same current passes every point: charge cannot pile up or leak away.
claims.source: Kirchhoff's current law (conservation of charge). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 27 (Circuits), resistances in series.

claims.text: With a 6 V battery and two 6 ohm bulbs the current is 0.50 A; the battery slider gives I = V / 12 ohm (0.17 A at 2 V up to 1.00 A at 12 V, in 2 V steps).
claims.source: Ohm's law for two 6 ohm resistors in series: I = V / 12. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 V give 0.167, 0.333, 0.50, 0.667, 0.833, 1.00 A (shown to 2 d.p.). Each bulb drops I x 6 = V / 2: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 V. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: I = V/12 at 2,4,6,8,10,12 V = 0.17, 0.33, 0.50, 0.67, 0.83, 1.00 A; per-bulb drop V/2 = 1..6 V; matches Demo.tsx amps() and drop.

claims.text: Each identical bulb takes half the battery voltage: 3 V each from 6 V. The voltage drop is the energy each coulomb of charge hands over.
claims.source: V = I R = 0.50 x 6 = 3.0 V per bulb; Kirchhoff's voltage law, 3 + 3 = 6 V. Voltage as energy per unit charge: Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 24 and 27.

claims.text: The battery and wires are ideal (no internal resistance) and the bulbs are treated as fixed 6 ohm resistors; real bulb filaments change resistance as they heat.
claims.source: Stated idealisation. Filament resistance rises with temperature (Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 26, resistivity and temperature).

claims.text: The moving dots show the direction of conventional current (out of the battery's + end); the same number pass every spot, their speed is a picture of the current's size (not the real drift speed of electrons, which move the other way), and their brightness fading after each bulb is a picture of the energy handed over.
claims.source: Conventional current direction is defined from + to -; electrons drift opposite, at speeds of order 0.1 mm/s in typical wires (Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 26, drift speed). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Checked against the stage: battery drawn with long plate and '+' on top, dots path runs up from it (conventional current); dot speed scales with I/0.5; dot opacity steps 1, 0.5, 0.12 after each bulb (qualitative picture); electron drift in ordinary wires is of order 0.1 mm/s (Halliday-Resnick-Walker ch. 26).

claims.text: A bigger battery voltage raises the current everywhere in the loop at once.
claims.source: From c1 and c2: I = V / 12 ohm is a single value for the whole loop.

claims.text: Amps measure charge passing per second; volts measure the energy each charge carries (or hands over).
claims.source: SI definitions: 1 A = 1 C/s; 1 V = 1 J/C (BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed.). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): SI: ampere = coulomb per second, volt = joule per coulomb (BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed.). 'Energy each charge carries' is read as energy per unit charge.

recall.question: Three identical bulbs are in series on one battery. The current into the first bulb is 0.30 A. What is the current coming out of the third bulb?
recall.why: In a single loop the same current passes every point; the bulbs use up energy, not current.
